To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
diabetes mellitus is associated with breast cancer in women.

1) the prevalence of breast cancer is higher in diabetic than in non-diabetic patients; 2) diabetic patients with breast cancer are younger, have a lower BMI and a higher prevalence of ER-negative tumors; 3) diabetes is associated with a poorer outcome in breast cancer patients; 4) diabetes increases the risk of recurrence and death in breast cancer patients, especially those who are overweight or obese.
diabetes increases breast cancer risk and that the risk is higher in women who are obese and/or who have a family history of breast cancer.

the role of insulin in breast development and the possible link between diabetes and breast cancer.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the breast cancer incidence is higher in diabetics, the prognosis is poorer and the treatment is similar to that in non-diabetics.
the presence of diabetes mellitus in a patient with a breast lump is a risk factor for the presence of malignancy, but it is not an independent predictor of breast cancer.
breast lumps in diabetes mellitus are not common, but are not rare, either.
The main takeaway from our work is that

breast cancer is not a single disease, but rather a group of diseases, and we need to be able to identify the different subtypes of breast cancer to understand why some women do well with a certain treatment and some do not, said senior author Matthew Ellis, M.D., Ph.D., director of the Lester and Sue Smith Breast Center and chair of Breast Medical Oncology at Baylor College of Medicine.

breast cancer screening should be considered for women with diabetes, even if they are not in the high-risk category.
